An hors d'oeuvre is a small, bite-sized food item served before the main meal begins. Think of it as a little snack or taster that guests eat while waiting for the actual dinner or lunch to be served.

The key word here is small — an hors d'oeuvre is never a full dish. It is designed to be eaten in one or two bites, often while standing up, holding a drink, and chatting with other guests.
When and Where Are They Served?

Hors d'oeuvres appear in situations like:

  • Cocktail parties or receptions, where there may not even be a sit-down meal — the hors d'oeuvres are the food of the evening.
  • Before a formal dinner, where guests mingle and snack while the main meal is being prepared.
  • Weddings, corporate events, or galas, where waitstaff walk around carrying trays of small bites for guests to pick from.
  • At home gatherings, where a host might put out small snacks before the dinner is ready.

The whole point is that hors d'oeuvres exist outside of and before the structured meal. They are the "bridge" between arriving and actually sitting down to eat.

Hors d'oeuvres are typically:

  • Small — one or two bites at most.
  • Easy to handle — they're meant to be eaten without a knife and fork, often with just a toothpick, a small napkin, or your fingers.
  • Neatly presented — they tend to look elegant and well-crafted, not like a casual snack tossed in a bowl.
  • Hot or cold — both are perfectly normal.
  • Savory most of the time, though sweet versions exist.

They might be served on small plates, on trays carried by waiters, or arranged on a table for guests to help themselves.

To make this very concrete, here are things you would call an hors d'oeuvre:

  • A small cracker topped with cream cheese and smoked salmon
  • A stuffed mushroom cap
  • A mini quiche (a tiny egg-and-pastry bite)
  • A skewer of grilled chicken with dipping sauce
  • Shrimp cocktail (a single shrimp with sauce on the side)
  • Bruschetta (a small slice of toasted bread with tomatoes on top)
  • A deviled egg
  • A spring roll cut into small pieces

Notice what all of these have in common: they are small, self-contained, easy to pick up, and satisfying in just a couple of bites.
How Is It Different from Similar Words?

This is where many learners get confused. Here is a clear breakdown:

Hors d'oeuvre vs. Appetizer
These two words are often used interchangeably in everyday conversation, and that is fine. But strictly speaking, there is a difference. An appetizer is the first course of a sit-down meal — you're already at the table when it arrives. An hors d'oeuvre is served before you even sit down. So all hors d'oeuvres can loosely be called appetizers, but not all appetizers are hors d'oeuvres.

Hors d'oeuvre vs. Canapé
A canapé is actually a specific type of hors d'oeuvre. It always has a base — usually a small piece of bread, toast, or a cracker — with a topping on it. So a canapé is always an hors d'oeuvre, but an hors d'oeuvre is not always a canapé (because many hors d'oeuvres have no bread base at all).

Hors d'oeuvre vs. Amuse-bouche
An amuse-bouche is a single, tiny dish that a chef sends out to diners in a fine-dining restaurant, purely as a gift and a preview of the chef's style. You don't order it; it just arrives. An hors d'oeuvre is more broadly any small pre-meal bite, not necessarily in a fancy restaurant context.

The plural of hors d'oeuvre can be written two ways, and both are correct:

  • Hors d'oeuvre (unchanged — the same word works for both singular and plural)
  • Hors d'oeuvres (with an added "s" at the end)

In English, you will see both forms used, and neither is wrong.
How It Is Used in Sentences

• "The guests were enjoying the hors d'oeuvres while waiting for dinner to be served."
  • "She passed around a tray of hors d'oeuvres at the party."
  • "The cocktail hour featured an impressive spread of hors d'oeuvres."
  • "Can I offer you an hors d'oeuvre before we sit down?"

An hors d'oeuvre is a small, elegant, bite-sized food item served before the main meal, typically at a party or formal gathering.

If you remember just that one sentence, you have the word nailed.
